blocks.text: Picture this: you are building a habit tracker and you want to show a full calendar grid for the current month, every single day already laid out, even before the user has logged anything. Or maybe you are pulling stock prices and you need a complete list of every trading day in the last quarter, so you can line your real data up against it and instantly see which days you are missing. Both of these are the same underlying problem. You need a clean, complete, evenly spaced sequence of dates to work against, and pandas hands you exactly that with one function, pd.date_range().

This lesson walks through pd.date_range() end to end: how to tell it where to start and stop, how to control the spacing between the dates it generates, and the one use case that comes up again and again in real data work, using a complete date range to catch a time series that is quietly missing rows without you ever noticing.

blocks.alt: Start date and end date feeding into date_range which produces a full evenly spaced sequence
blocks.caption: The whole function in one picture: two boundaries in, a complete sequence out.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

pd.date_range() is pandas' tool for generating a complete, evenly spaced sequence of dates or times. You give it a bit of information about where the sequence should start and stop and how far apart each date should be, and it hands back a DatetimeIndex full of Timestamp objects, the exact same building blocks covered in the Timestamp lesson earlier in this module. If that lesson is fresh in your mind, this will feel familiar immediately: every date that comes out of date_range is a real Timestamp, not a plain string, so the whole pandas datetime toolkit, weekday names, month arithmetic, timezone handling, works on each one automatically.
This one function ends up doing three different jobs depending on what you need at the moment.

items: Generating a synthetic time series from scratch, useful for testing, prototyping, or building demo data before real data exists.
Building a complete date index that you can attach to a dataset or hand to a chart as its x axis.
Reindexing an existing dataset onto that complete index, which is the single most practical use case in this entire lesson, covered in depth later on.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', end='2024-01-05')

blocks.text: Run that and pandas gives you back a DatetimeIndex holding five dates, January 1st through January 5th, one for every day in between. No loops, no manual date math, no off by one errors to worry about.
2. The Core Parameters: Start, End, and Periods

date_range is built around three ideas: start, end, and periods. start and end are the two boundary dates you want the sequence to span. periods is a specific count of dates you want, counted forward from a starting point, used instead of a fixed end date. The genuinely useful thing to understand up front is that you almost never need to specify all three at once.
2.1 Start and End

The most natural way to think about date_range is a window with two edges. You tell pandas where the window opens and where it closes, and it fills in everything in between at whatever spacing you ask for.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

dates = pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', end='2024-01-05')
print(dates)

# DatetimeIndex(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-03', '2024-01-04',
#                '2024-01-05'],
#               dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='D')

blocks.alt: Five sequential dates from January 1 through January 5 chained together
blocks.caption: start equals Jan 1, end equals Jan 5, default daily spacing produces exactly these five dates.

blocks.text: 2.2 Start and Periods

Sometimes you do not have a natural end date in mind, you just know how many dates you want. That is exactly what periods is for. Give date_range a start and a count, and it walks forward that many steps and stops, no end required at all.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

dates = pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', periods=5)
print(dates)

# DatetimeIndex(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-03', '2024-01-04',
#                '2024-01-05'],
#               dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='D')

blocks.text: Notice this produces the exact same five dates as the start and end example above. start='2024-01-01', end='2024-01-05' and start='2024-01-01', periods=5 describe the same sequence in two different vocabularies, one anchored on a boundary date, the other anchored on a count.

blocks.alt: A starting date and a periods count of three feeding into date_range producing three dates
blocks.caption: start equals Jan 1, periods equals 3 walks forward exactly three steps, no end date needed.

blocks.text: 2.3 Why You Only Need Two of Three

start, end, and periods are three ways of describing the same shape, a beginning, an ending, and a length. If you know any two of those, basic arithmetic gives you the third, and pandas does exactly that arithmetic for you once it knows the freq you want. That is why the normal habit is to supply exactly two of the three and let pandas figure out the rest.

blocks.content: {"headers":["You provide","Pandas figures out","A good time to use it"],"rows":[["start and end","How many dates fit at the given frequency","You already know the exact window you care about"],["start and periods","The end date","You know how many points you need but do not have a natural end date in mind"],["end and periods","The start date","You are counting backward from a known end date"]]}

blocks.title: Just pick any two
blocks.content: You will almost never explicitly hand pandas all three of start, end, and periods at once. If you do supply all three and they do not line up with the freq you gave, pandas raises an error rather than silently guessing which one you actually meant, so there is no real upside to overspecifying it.

blocks.text: 3. The freq Parameter

freq is the single most important parameter on date_range. It controls the spacing between every generated date, and changing it changes the entire character of the sequence you get back, even if start and end stay exactly the same. Left unset, freq defaults to D, one date per calendar day.
3.1 Daily Frequency
freq='D' is the default, and it is the one you will reach for most often. Every single calendar day between start and end gets its own entry in the resulting DatetimeIndex, with nothing skipped.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', end='2024-01-05', freq='D')

blocks.alt: Five consecutive weekday labeled nodes spaced one after another
blocks.caption: freq equals D ticks off every single calendar day in a row, nothing skipped.

blocks.text: 3.2 Weekly Frequency

freq='W' keeps only one date per week instead of one per day. By default it anchors on Sundays, so across a full month you end up with roughly four dates instead of thirty, one per Sunday that falls inside the range.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', end='2024-01-31', freq='W')

# DatetimeIndex(['2024-01-07', '2024-01-14', '2024-01-21', '2024-01-28'],
#               dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='W-SUN')

blocks.alt: Four week labeled nodes spaced far apart representing weekly frequency
blocks.caption: freq equals W keeps only one date per week across the same span, four points instead of thirty one.

blocks.text: 3.3 Month End Versus Month Start

freq='M' and freq='MS' look almost identical at a glance and generate completely different dates. freq='M' anchors on the last calendar day of each month, so it can land on the 28th, 29th, 30th, or 31st depending on the month. freq='MS' anchors on the first day of each month instead, always the 1st, no exceptions.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', end='2024-04-01', freq='M')
# DatetimeIndex(['2024-01-31', '2024-02-29', '2024-03-31'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='M')

pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', end='2024-04-01', freq='MS')
# DatetimeIndex(['2024-01-01', '2024-02-01', '2024-03-01', '2024-04-01'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='MS')

blocks.alt: Two small chains of three dates side by side, one landing on month end dates, one landing on month start dates
blocks.caption: Month end and month start anchor on opposite edges of the same months, a genuinely easy pair to mix up.

blocks.title: M and MS are not the same thing
blocks.content: This is one of the most commonly confused frequency codes in all of pandas. Mixing M and MS up quietly shifts every date in your range by roughly a month, and the resulting bug is easy to miss because both produce a perfectly reasonable looking monthly series, just anchored on the wrong edge of the month.

blocks.text: 3.4 Hourly Frequency

freq='H' steps forward one hour at a time instead of one day at a time. It is what you reach for once your data gets more granular than a single day, sensor readings, server logs, or anything else logged multiple times per day.
3.5 A Quick Reference Table
Remembering every frequency code by heart is not realistic, and nobody actually does it. Looking one up when you need it is the normal workflow, so keep a table like this one within reach.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Code","Meaning","Typical use"],"rows":[["D","Every calendar day","Daily logs, daily sales, the general purpose default"],["B","Every business day, weekends skipped","Trading data, business reporting"],["W","Once a week, Sunday anchored by default","Weekly summaries, weekly reports"],["M","Last calendar day of each month","Month end financial close, month end snapshots"],["MS","First calendar day of each month","Billing cycles, subscription periods that start on the first"],["Q","Last calendar day of each quarter","Quarterly financials"],["H","Every hour","Hourly sensor readings, hourly traffic"],["T or min","Every minute","High frequency application or server logs"],["Y or A","Last calendar day of each year","Annual summaries"]]}

blocks.alt: Five labeled nodes listing the codes D, W, M, MS, and H each in a different color
blocks.caption: The handful of frequency codes you will reach for constantly, worth keeping visible until they stick.

blocks.text: 4. Worked Example: Daily, Weekly, and Monthly Side by Side
To make the spacing difference completely concrete, generate the exact same calendar month, July 2024, at three different frequencies and compare what comes back.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

daily = pd.date_range(start='2024-07-01', end='2024-07-31', freq='D')
print(len(daily))
# 31

weekly = pd.date_range(start='2024-07-01', end='2024-07-31', freq='W')
print(len(weekly))
print(weekly)

# 4
# DatetimeIndex(['2024-07-07', '2024-07-14', '2024-07-21', '2024-07-28'],
#               dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='W-SUN')

monthly = pd.date_range(start='2024-07-01', end='2024-07-31', freq='M')
print(monthly)

# DatetimeIndex(['2024-07-31'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='M')

blocks.content: {"headers":["Frequency","Code","Dates generated across July 2024"],"rows":[["Daily","D","31 dates, one for every single day in the month"],["Weekly","W","4 dates, one per week, landing on the Sundays inside the month"],["Month end","M","1 date, just July 31st, the last day of the month"]]}

blocks.text: Same start, same end, three completely different results. That is the entire point of freq, it decides how densely pandas fills in the space you gave it.
5. Business Day Frequency

Financial and business data usually does not care about Saturday and Sunday, the market is closed, the office is empty, and those two calendar dates are not real trading or business days at all. Rather than generating them and filtering them out yourself, freq='B' skips weekends automatically while it builds the sequence.
Notice July 6th and July 7th, a Saturday and Sunday, never show up at all. The sequence jumps straight from Friday the 5th to Monday the 8th, exactly how a trading calendar behaves.

blocks.alt: Thursday Friday Monday Tuesday chained together with Saturday and Sunday shown separately as skipped
blocks.caption: freq equals B walks Thu, Fri, then jumps straight to Mon, Sat and Sun never appear in the sequence.

blocks.title: Business days are not the same as holidays
blocks.content: freq='B' only knows about Saturday and Sunday. It has no idea that a given Monday might be a public holiday, so if a market or office is closed on a weekday for a holiday, that date still shows up in a freq='B' range. For that level of accuracy you would reach for pandas' CustomBusinessDay with an actual holiday calendar attached to it.

blocks.text: 6. Revealing Gaps by Reindexing

Here is the single most practical real world use case for date_range: reindexing an incomplete time series onto a complete one to reveal gaps. A time series that is missing dates entirely, not NaN values, actually missing rows, looks deceptively complete right up until you reindex it onto a proper complete date_range. Then, suddenly, NaN rows appear exactly where dates were missing, and you can finally see what was hiding.
6.1 Why an Incomplete Time Series Looks Deceptively Complete

Imagine a small set of logged readings. Nothing about it looks broken, the dates are sorted, there is no NaN anywhere, and if you were skimming it quickly you would probably assume every day got logged.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

logged_dates = pd.to_datetime(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-04', '2024-01-05'])
print(logged_dates)

# DatetimeIndex(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-04', '2024-01-05'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)

blocks.text: Look closely and January 3rd is nowhere in that list. It was simply never recorded, there is no placeholder for it, no NaN, no empty string, just a quiet absence that a quick glance will not catch.

blocks.alt: Four dates chained in a row that look perfectly sequential at a glance
blocks.caption: Four rows, sorted, no NaN in sight, but Jan 3 quietly never made it into this list at all.

blocks.text: 6.2 Reindexing onto a Complete Date Range

Build a complete date_range covering the same span and reindex the series onto it. Every date that used to be silently absent now becomes an explicit row, holding a NaN, because there is no value to fill it with.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

series = pd.Series([10, 12, 9, 14], index=logged_dates)
full_range = pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', end='2024-01-05', freq='D')
print(series.reindex(full_range))

# 2024-01-01    10.0
# 2024-01-02    12.0
# 2024-01-03     NaN
# 2024-01-04     9.0
# 2024-01-05    14.0
# Freq: D, dtype: float64

blocks.alt: Five dates in a row with the third one highlighted red and labeled NaN, the rest green
blocks.caption: Reindexing onto a complete date_range slots Jan 3 back in as an explicit NaN row you can finally see.

blocks.title: Missing rows are not the same as NaN values
blocks.content: Before you reindex, a missing date does not exist anywhere in your data, there is no row for it, nothing to inspect, nothing that visibly looks wrong. After you reindex onto a complete date_range, that same missing date becomes an explicit row holding a NaN. Nothing about the underlying data changed, only your ability to see the gap changed, which is exactly why this is worth doing as a habit, not just when you already suspect something is missing.

blocks.text: 6.3 Handling the Gaps You Just Revealed

Once a gap is visible as a NaN row, you get to make a deliberate decision about it instead of never knowing it existed in the first place. The right choice depends entirely on what the missing date actually means for your data.

code.content:
reindexed = series.reindex(full_range)

# option 1: treat the gap as genuinely zero
filled_zero = reindexed.fillna(0)

# option 2: carry the last known value forward
filled_forward = reindexed.ffill()

# option 3: estimate a smooth value between neighbors
filled_interp = reindexed.interpolate()

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","What it does","When it fits"],"rows":[["fillna with a fixed value","Replaces every NaN with the same value, often 0","The gap genuinely means zero activity, like a store that was closed"],["ffill","Carries the last known value forward into the gap","The value probably did not change much, like a slowly moving sensor reading"],["interpolate","Estimates a smooth value between the point before and after the gap","The underlying quantity trends smoothly, like temperature or price"],["dropna","Removes the gap rows entirely","You just wanted to detect and discard incomplete rows, not fill them"]]}

blocks.alt: A red NaN row flowing into a fillna or interpolate step and out as a clean green value
blocks.caption: Once a gap is visible as NaN, you get to decide how to handle it instead of never knowing it was there.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: A Sales Dataset With Missing Days

Put the whole technique together on something closer to a real dataset. Say you are tracking daily units sold for the first ten days of July 2024, but the logging pipeline dropped a couple of days along the way.

Eight rows, sorted by date, every value present, nothing about this table waves any kind of red flag. July 4th and July 8th are simply not there, and unless you already knew to expect ten days of data, there is nothing here that tells you two of them went missing.

blocks.alt: Four sales figures chained together looking like a complete short run of days
blocks.caption: Eight rows of daily sales that look like a complete window at a glance, no NaN, nothing obviously broken.

blocks.text: Reindexed onto a full ten day date_range, July 4th and July 8th snap into view as explicit NaN rows. That is the gap, made visible, exactly where the original table hid it.

blocks.alt: A short run of sales figures with one entry highlighted red and labeled NaN among the rest
blocks.caption: The same window reindexed onto a full date_range, one of the missing days shows up as an explicit NaN you can now act on.

code.content:
# a missing sales record is not automatically the same as zero sales,
# it might just mean the pipeline failed to log that day
sales_complete['units_sold'] = sales_complete['units_sold'].interpolate()
print(sales_complete.loc['2024-07-03':'2024-07-05'])

blocks.text: Here interpolate() makes more sense than filling with zero, a sales number of zero would claim the store sold nothing at all on those days, when the far more likely explanation is a gap in the logging pipeline, not a gap in actual sales. Reindexing did the hard part, surfacing the gap in the first place. Choosing how to fill it is a judgment call you can now make on purpose.
8. Summary

items: pd.date_range() generates a complete, evenly spaced DatetimeIndex full of Timestamp objects.
You only ever need to supply two of start, end, and periods, pandas works out the third.
freq controls the spacing, D for daily, W for weekly, M for month end, MS for month start, H for hourly, B for business days, and there are plenty more worth looking up when you need them.
M anchors on the last day of the month, MS anchors on the first, mixing them up is a classic and easy mistake.
Reindexing an incomplete time series onto a complete date_range is the fastest way to catch dates that are silently missing rather than just holding a NaN.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Parameter","What it controls"],"rows":[["start","The first date in the sequence"],["end","The last date in the sequence"],["periods","A fixed count of dates instead of a fixed end"],["freq","The spacing between each generated date"]]}

blocks.title: Keep the frequency table bookmarked
blocks.content: Nobody keeps every frequency code memorized, and you should not try to either. Looking up whether you need M or MS, or whether W anchors on Sunday, is completely normal, even for people who use pandas every day. What matters is knowing date_range exists and reaching for it the moment you suspect a time series might have silent gaps in it.
